html:
A strong earthquake that struck Venezuela on 26 March 1812, Maundy Thursday, destroying much of Caracas and other towns such as La Guaira, Barquisimeto, San Felipe and Mérida. An estimated 15,000 to 20,000 people died.

It came at the worst time for the young republic. Venezuela had declared independence from Spain in 1811, one of the first steps of the Spanish American wars of independence. The quake struck mostly towns held by the patriots, while royalist areas suffered less, and it fell on Maundy Thursday, the same holy day on which the revolt in Caracas had begun in 1810. Royalist priests preached that it was God's punishment for rebellion.

The young Simón Bolívar is said to have climbed onto the ruins and shouted that if nature opposed them, they would fight nature too. Within months the First Republic collapsed and Bolívar fled. He came back the next year to keep fighting.
